speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PENSIONS-OLD AGE AND BLIND-FILING OF LIENS
speechtext:
1.	In what provinces are liens filed against the property of old age and blind pensioners?
'\Ir. Howe.]
2.	Is the filing of such liens the subject of any arrangement or agreement between the provinces and federal government?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PENSIONS-OLD AGE AND BLIND-FILING OF LIENS
speechtext:
1.	The provinces of Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have the power to control property owned by old age pensioners and blind pensioners under the authority of provincial legislation. At the time of the last dominion examination of the provincial pension accounts, these provinces appeared to be following the general practice of filing liens or registration notices as authorized by their legislation.
2.	There is no agreement and no regulation regarding the filing of such liens, other than the general agreement of each pension authority to administer pensions in accordance with the act and the regulations. Subsection 3 of section 9 of the Old Age Pensions Act provides as follows:
A pension authority shall be entitled to recover out of the estate of any deceased pensioner, as a debt due by the pensioner to such authority, the sum of the pension payments made to such pensioner from time to time, together with interest at the rate of five per cent per annum, compounded annually, but no claim shall be made by a pension authority for the recovery of such debt directly or indirectly out of any part of the pensioner's estate which passes by will or on an intestacy to any other pensioner or to any person who has, since the grant of such pension or for the last three years during which such pension has continued to be paid, regularly contributed to the support of the pensioner by the payment of money or otherwise to an extent which, having regard to the means of the person so having contributed, is considered by the pension authority to be reasonable.
There has been some legal doubt as to whether this clause was mandatory or permissive in its effect. For some time the dominion has followed the legal opinion that the section indicated an intention on the part of parliament that recoveries should be made and that as a matter of sound administration, it should be regarded as a statutory direction to the pension authorities to make recoveries in the ordinary course. More recently we have been advised that while the drafting may leave some legal doubt, nevertheless the subsection is, strictly speaking, permissive. The provincial pension authorities have, as indicated in the answer to question 1, followed different policies, some have refused to follow the administrative requirement of making claims against the estates of deceased pensioners, others have suggested that it might be desirable either to discontinue making claims in all cases or to limit claims to the larger estates. In view of this situation, the provincial pension authorities are being

Questions
advised that whether or not recovery should be made from estates where the net value does not exceed two thousand dollars will be left entirely to their discretion.

1.	The following officials of the Department of Finance, Department of External Affairs, the Bank of Canada and foreign exchange control board took part in the drafting of the "Tentative draft proposals of Canadian experts for an international exchange union":
R.	B. Bryce, W. C. Clark, J. J. Deutsch.W.A. Mackintosh, L. Rasminsky, N. A. Robertson, G. F. Towers.
2 and 3. The proposals were drafted to serve as a basis for the comments and suggestions to be made in regard to the American and British currency proposals by the Canadian experts who were to attend the discussions on this subject in Washington. Several of these Canadian officials participated in these discussions as a result of an invitation which the Minister of Finance, as he explained to the house on July 12 last year, had received from the Secretary of the United States Treasury to send technical experts to Washington for an informal discussion of the proposals for an international stabilization fund prepared by officials in the United States treasury. Those who took part in the drafting of the "tentative draft proposals" did not receive any instructions or terms of reference, as it was definitely understood that the experts in discussing this question, were to do so solely on their own responsibility with a view to exploring the possibility of reaching agreements on proposals that could be recommended to governments in order to solve the problem of post-war monetary instability.

speakeroldname: Mr. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I should like this afternoon, with the permission of the committee, to deal with two subject matters which have to do with the war appropriation bill, which we are discussing at the moment. The first relates to the purchasing policy of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and the second to the renegotiation of contracts.
Before I go on to these I may be permitted, Mr. Chairman, to express to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) the pleasure of the committee in his return to our midst. He has just come back from important duties overseas, and I know I express the feelings of the committee when I say that we are all delighted to find him in such excellent health.
(Translation): Mr. Chairman, I am happy to welcome back the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) whom I see occupying his seat. Some time ago, the house expressed sympathy in the deep loss which he experienced; to-day, we are happy to see him in good health and so well recovered.
(Text) Last year when I was reporting on the purchasing policy of the Department, of Munitions and Supply I referred to the manner in which contracts were awarded in the department, the methods adopted to reduce costs and control profits, the controls exercised over munitions contracts generally, and the reduction in prices consequent upon these controls. At that time I emphasized the fact that the department sought always to obtain fixed prices. The department was interested in asking, for tenders in order that competitive bidding might be set up, and by that method contracts obtained of a fixed price type. The department then felt, and still feels, that the cheapest method of obtaining production, from the standpoint both of costs and of profits, is through negotiation of short term contracts on a fixed price basis. I gave the reasons for that at the time: First, because many of those contracts were for equipment never made before in this country. Obviously in such cases it was impossible to obtain fixed, prices until production was well under way. Second, because of the frequent changes in the design of equipment while it was in production; and third, because the department is not always able to obtain full, accurate and up-to-date knowledge of the contractor's costs. For these and other reasons it is not always possible to obtain fixed prices; hence we have to get variations and modifications, such as the ceiling price, the contract price, the cost plus percentage, and the unit fee arrangement. I said that these were temporary devices only which were being used pending the day when it would be found possible to negotiate fixed price contracts. I explained how, because of the checks and-controls exercised on costs, it was possible to make substantial reduction in prices. I am happy to report to-day that in the department wo have made much progress towards fixed price contracts, and away from variations and modifications of them.
War Appropriation-Supplies

In the Department of Munitions and Supply there are five large purchasing branches. These, of course, are not all-inclusive; but in these five branches the vast majority of war equipment is purchased through the channels of Munitions and Supply. These five branches are: (1) the general purchasing branch; (2) the defence projects construction branch; (3) the munitions contracts branch; (4) the aircraft division, and (5) the shipbuilding division.
The general purchasing branch has to do with general purchases, such as the purchases of personal equipment, medical stores, food supplies, miscellaneous goods of that type. With but very few exceptions all the purchases in that branch are on the fixed price basis. I believe I am safe in saying that over ninety-nine per cent of the purchases made in the general purchasing branch are for fixed prices.
The same thing can be said of all contracts awarded in recent months by the defence projects construction branch. I hold in my hand a report from that branch which shows the comparison of cost plus contracts to total contracts awarded there and their value, from the first quarter of 1940 to the last quarter of 1943. During the four quarters of 1942 the percentage of cost plus contracts to the total was thirty-two per cent, and during the four quarters of 1943 the percentage of cost plus contracts to the total was 9-75 per cent, a substantial reduction.
The automotive contracts have now been converted entirely to fixed prices. The committee will remember that last year when I reported I stated that most of these contracts were on the ceiling price basis. To-day I am able to report that practically all contracts with the automotive companies are on the fixed price basis. The same conversion to fixed prices obtains in the munitions contracts branch where our knowledge of costs and manufacturing technique has enabled us to change over in great part.
A report covering this branch, which I have before me and which is as at January 31, 1944, shows that of a total of 15,267 contracts granted in this branch only 8-94 per cent were on a cost plus contracts basis. During the year 1943 of a total amount of contracts of $1,200,000,000, the estimated value of cost plus contracts was $379,825,806. The same position does not obtain in the aircraft division. It is not possible to put aircraft contracts on the fixed price basis, because of the constant and everlasting change in design. There is no known way of determining the efficiency of aircraft except by use in combat;
[Mr. Chevrier.l
hence we must ask our manufacturers to make frequent changes in design of equipment. For these reasons aircraft contracts must be on the cost plus basis, and they will in all probability remain that way.
Changes with reference to ship contracts have also had to be made. Originally, as the committee knows-[DOT]

Would the hon.
member permit a question?

speechtext: Yes.
What is the basis of the cost plus in the production of aircraft? What is the percentage of profit allowed to the operating companies?

speechtext:
I must say I have not the facts before me. I have not a report of that branch as I have of the other branches, but I shall be glad to get my hon. friend an answer.
I was saying that originally all ship contracts were let at fixed prices with allowances for wage and freight differentials all across the country. It was found, however, that there were wide differences in the efficiencies of the yards for a variety of reasons. Accordingly a price on which one yard might make a slight profit or another might sustain a loss might yield an undue profit to a third yard.
Apart from this, our engineers were faced with a constant stream of extras and modifications to original designs, and the problems of adjusting prices to cover these changes became involved and difficult. Accordingly, it was decided late in 1942 to readjust all contracts from a certain date either to cost plus a fixed fee or to a basis of cost plus a fixed fee per ship, plus a bonus for reduction of cost below a target. The fixed-fee plan no doubt penalized the two or three yards of highest efficiency, but the view was taken that looking at their operations as a whole, their efficiency had been given due but not excessive recognition. The committee will realize that placing ships on the basis of cost plus a fixed fee, plus a bonus for reducing costs below a target, is the next best thing to a fixed price contract, in that it preserves an incentive to cost reduction even if in a modified form.

On the whole, the purchasing policy of the department has been carried out along sound businesslike lines. It has led to substantial reductions in the prices of war materiel.
Let me for a moment turn to another angle of this policy. We have heard a lot about the Labour government in Australia. We have been told frequently in this house and outside that the policies of the party led by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar are similar to those governing the commonwealth of Australia.
But that is not a fact.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says it is a fact. I do not believe I am misquoting him when I say that. In any event I should like to examine for a moment the purchasing methods adopted in the commonwealth in order to see how they deal with contractors and manufacturers.
Some months ago, I believe it was in June, 1943, the government of Australia set up a contracts advisory panel. It was created to investigate the cost plus profit system of the commonwealth contracts. The report has recently been published and its recommendations have been adopted by the government, as announced in a statement by Prime Minister Curtin in November of 1943. An examination of this report will show that the purchasing methods of the commonwealth are similar to ours and, in fact, in many instances, they are much more generous to the manufacturer than we in Canada are.
The report contains three outstanding features: the cost plus profit contract, the target price contract, and the fixed price contract.
It recommends that the cost plus system whilst essential during the initial period of great urgency and cost uncertainty, should be abandoned in favour of fixed price contracts
for all items for which an opportunity has been given of establishing costs. Let us examine these three features:
1.	On a cost plus profit contract:
The Australians have decided the profit should be 24 per cent on materials plus 7i per cent on labour and overhead. This averages about 5-6 per cent in ordinary run of war materiel.
In Canada, our view is that on ordinary cost plus contracts the profit should be 5 per cent, with something better in exceptional cases where unusual skill or services are provided, and somewhat less where production is of a very routine character.
This relates only to the manufacture of items in which materials employed are purchased. It does not apply in the case of, say, a mining company which produces everything from the underground operation through the extraction, refining and working up into a highly finished production.
In the management of government-owned plants such as, for instance, Defence Industries Limited, Canadian Car Munitions, the fee is very much less.
2.	Target price:
Our usual basis on a target price contract is cost plus a 5 per cent fixed fee plus 25 per cent of the saving below the target- although we have some in which a lesser percentage is allowed and a very few in which a graded profit sharing allowance in excess of 25 per cent is provided. In Australia, they use a 4 per cent fixed fee, plus a graded scale as follows:	[DOT]

3.	Fixed prices:
On fixed prices, the Australians come to the same conclusion as we do, and they strongly recommend that these be used wherever possible.
The Prime Minister of Australia in November of 1943 had this to say on the subject:
The war cabinet to-day considered the first report submitted by the contracts advisory panel in respect of the cost-plus profit and other methods of contracting. All departments engaged in the purchase of government supplies, or undertaking government works, will be instructed to move away from the cost-plus system of contracting in as many cases as possible.
It was impossible to avoid the adoption of cost-plus contracting in the early stages of the war, because a great proportion of the supplies, particularly of munitions, were entirely new to Australian manufacturers, and it would have been unreasonable to expect contractors to give firm prices. If that had been done, the contractors would quite justifiably have allowed for unknown contingencies, and to the extent to which these failed to occur unduly high profits would have resulted. Now, however, both the buying departments and the suppliers have the experience necessary to determine fair and reasonable prices, and when these have been fixed they will not be disturbed.
I consider that the time has come when the government should secure fixed prices whenever it can, and that the suspicion inherent in all cost-plus profit contracts, that the more a job costs, the more the contractor makes should be removed.
The government realizes, moreover, that even now some classes of work, such as the overhaul of aircraft and the repair of ships, will need to be done on the basis of actual cost, plus some form of remuneration. The remuneration will be based on a percentage of cost only where no better method of determining the profit margin can be fixed.
From this it will be seen that the methods adopted in Australia are very similar to our own, in fact, the Australians are far more generous to the contractor than we in Canada are.
I need hardly add that the Australian purchasing policy is predicated on the assumption that the munitions programme should be carried out by private industry, and that private industry is entitled to a fair and reasonable profit for its effort.
I would suggest to the leader of the C.C.F. party that the similarity between the policies of his party and those of the government of Australia are not as apparent as he would lead us to believe.
I should like to deal for a moment with the subject of renegotiation, but before doing so I should like to table, with the permission of the committee, a manual on termination of contracts. We in the Department of Munitions and Supply have had our attention
[Mr. Chevrier.l
directed chiefly toward the war programme, but we have realized that there will be a post-war period and with that in mind we have reviewed the termination clauses of our contracts and have set up a procedure in the department which has to do with the claims of contractors and subcontractors. I am sure that this document will be of interest to the members of the committee.
The important thing in the fixed price type of contract is that there should be a sound basis for arriving at a fixed price. A prematurely fixed price based on inadequate data, is just as much a danger to be avoided as a cost plus percentage type.
It sometimes happens that with the best of information as to the costs, the best of intentions and the keenest negotiations, a fixed price ends up by yielding an undue profit to the manufacturer.
Such a profit may be due to the discovery by the manufacturer of some new type of material, or the development of other economies not previously visualized. It may also be due to the subsequent addition of new business from various sources leading to the spreading of the fixed overhead of the business over a much larger volume of output. Whenever this occurs, the department takes the view that the contractor in wartime should be content to give to the taxpayer the greater part of the benefit of the improved techniques, rather than retain them for himself. While the department appreciates the principle of the sanctity of contracts entered into between itself and its contractors, still it realizes that in wartime, there is a responsibility placed upon the minister to protect the taxpayer's money. For this reason, where it is shown that profits are unreasonable, the department renegotiates contracts.
Renegotiation is a retroactive price reduction after the contracts have been let and the goods purchased. This practice may be voluntary or compulsory. Its object is twofold: To lower the costs of war goods, and to prevent unreasonable profits on them.
Where the department becomes aware of an undue profit, and its officers are instructed to be constantly on the watch for such profits, it is the practice of the negotiating officers to seek price adjustments in order to bring the profit down to a fair and reasonable figure. In this regard, however, the view is held that some reasonable share of the products of the efficiency of the contractor should be left with him. In other words, on a renegotiation, whether entirely voluntary or taken on the initiative of the department, it is the practice to allow a reasonably larger profit margin than would be the case on a straight

War Appropriation-Supplies
rost-p'us-percentage contract. It is obvious that if this is not done, we would be taking away all incentive to cost reduction and all incentive to the assumption of manufacturing risks. In this connection, the report of the panel which investigated the contract policy of the Commonwealth of Australia has this to say:
Where the contract is substantial, the order placed should be for a quantity or for a period which will permit a review of the price after reasonable experience; or, alternatively, the order should be for the full quantity required with a condition that the price will be reviewed after the production of a stipulated quantity. The review of the price, however, should not be retrospective. When made, the revised price should not be so reduced as to deprive a contractor of the fruits of his efficiency or of the incentive to further reduce costs.
Two things should be noted here. The first is that renegotiation in Australia is never retroactive; that is to say, it never starts from the original date of the contract but rather from the date of the renegotiation. In Canada it is always retroactive. When we in Canada renegotiatiate a contract, the renegotiation price dates back to the original contract. Hence, on renegotiation also, the Australians are more generous with their contractors than we are. The next point to note is that renegotiation should always take care not to deprive the contractor of the incentive to further reduce costs.
This informal method of renegotiation has proved entirely effective and in no case has it been necessary for us to exercise the powers given by this house in section 13 of the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, to compel a contractor to return profits deemed to be unreasonable. The fact that these powers exists has been an influence in reaching a settlement in some cases, and we anticipate that in some instances we shall have to resort to them. I believe the committee will agree, however, that we should be as careful and as sparing in employing extraordinary measures as we possibly can. In the main we have met with excellent cooperation from the manufacturing community who fully realize the anti-social aspects of excessive profits on war contracts.
It is difficult to draw an exact line between various types of renegotiation. Circumstances vary in the individual instances and in many cases, an over-all readjustment in relation to a company's annual war business is made, even though the contracts for the year may include some cost-plus, some ceiling price, some target price, and some fixed-price contracts. We have made an attempt, however, to estimate the savings arising out of renegotiation of various types and are able to
point to a total of 8119,107,000, of which $66,691,000 covers instances of direct renegotiation and $52,416,000 arises chiefly out of price adjustments on ceiling price contracts.
These figures are undoubtedly conservative and do not take into account cases in which downward adjustments of prices have been made during the course of a contract, due to tne efforts of our negotiating offices or to the voluntary action of the manufacturer concerned.
These figures are not to be compared with the American figures for renegotiating which have been recorded as exceeding the five billion dollar mark. Our whole method of purchasing is different from that of the United States. In that country' a great volume of contracts in excess of 8100,000 are subject to being renegotiated, but, so far as we can ascertain, very much less attention is paid to the problems of setting the original price than we are accustomed to pay. The United States system appears to rely principally upon the powers of recapture of excessive profits, while in Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom the attempt is made to arrive at fair prices in the first place and to use the right of lecapture very sparingly, as above indicated. It is believed that this is the preferable method because no incentive exists for a manufacturer to cut costs and avoid wastages of materials and labour, if, under renegotiation powers, there will be left with him only the same amount of profit as would be the case were he to adopt a more easygoing attitude as regards cost reduction and cost control.
The problems of purchasing are not simple. They involve the exercise of a great deal of care and discriminating judgment.
One of the main jobs of the Department of Munitions and Supply is to get the maximum possible value for the taxpayer's dollar which involves not only seeing that profits are fair and reasonable, but that costs are driven down in every way possible.
The best proof of the wisdom of our policy is that to-day there exists a group of war contractors who are definitely cost conscious. Their interest in reducing costs is second only to their interest in production.
Since the outset of the war, there are three things which we have sought to do:
1.	To secure the maximum of output in the minimum of time.
2.	To secure all benefits of modern production and cost reduction technique.
3.	To keep profits under strict control.
I do not pretend that we have attained 100 per cent efficiency in all these, but all in all,
War Appropriation-Supplies

we are doing a good job in spending the taxpayer's money. We have tried to negotiate our contracts on a proper business-like basis. We maintain a close check on costs and profits through the audit system. We seek to improve manufacturing technique by daily contact between our production officers and our contractors, and we renegotiate our contracts when there is evidence of undue profit.
Our negotiating officers cannot always be right, but I can assure the house, from my personal knowledge, that there is in the department a group of able and hard-working men attempting honestly and without fear or favor, to administer their responsibilities in a way which should merit the favor of this house.
These men have succeeded in elaborating a purchasing policy that compares favorably with that of any of the united nations. These men are determined to stop war profiteering.
The minister in reporting to the house on Tuesday stated that from the inception, contracts awarded in the department amounted to 89,450,000,000.
With such an unprecedented outlay of public funds, after four and a half years of war, we in Canada have every reason to be proud of the fact that there have been few charges of graft and almost no charges of war profiteering. In the few cases where waste and dishonesty have been discovered, the department has moved quickly and effectively.
The department has one thing in view and that is to maintain a reputation for efficiency and honesty. I submit, sir, that it has established that reputation, and if it has succeeded in doing so, it is due not only to the purchasing methods to which I have referred a moment ago but also to the high and excellent calibre of the men in the department who administer these policies.

Mr. Chapman. I think we can all congratulate the hon. member who has just taken his seat upon the clarity with which he has expressed the point of view of the department.
I have not taken very much part in the debates on the war appropriation because the work has been apportioned among the various members of our group and it did not fall to my lot to engage in the discussions earlier.
I wish, however, to take this opportunity of saying that I am fully in accord with all the praise which has been given to the men in the armed forces, in the navy, the army, and the air force, and to the men and women who have contributed so largely and generously to Canada's industrial war effort.

The hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) spoke a few moments ago of Australia, and pointed out that from time to time we have had occasion to refer to Australia, New Zealand and the Labour party of Great Britain. He tried to draw some inferences from that regarding support for government policies. But I wish to point out that the government of Australia, under Mr. John Curtin, took office in November or late October, 1941, when the pattern of the war effort and of war contracts was already laid, and therefore that pattern had very largely to be followed no matter what the philosophic point of view of the members of that government happened to be. Besides, Australia had relatively little established industry when this war began compared with the very highly developed industry we had in Canada. Since then Australia, like ourselves, has established many new government owned and operated industries. Indeed, one of them was largely established before the war, the aeroplane industry, which also included, I believe, the manufacture of some aeroplane engines, but I am not sure of that. I do know that some new industries were established by the government as public enterprises, and I have read from time to time that the Australian government is carefully guarding the properties of the Australian people and is determined that when the war ends they shall be used for the production of civilian goods. In that respect the point of view of the Australian government, no matter what it may be as to the immediate question of making contracts, is radically different from the .point of view that has. been expressed in this house on behalf of the government.
As to generosity in the making of contracts, let me say this. They have a lower management fee and a greater participation, if costs are reduced, in the amount of the surplus attained, and it seems to me that is an incentive which under private business practice any government might well consider. I agree with the hon. member for Stormont that individuals engaged in a public service, whether in the employ of the government or as contractors making an essential commodity for war purposes, whether in public or in private enterprise, are entitled to fair remuneration for the services so rendered, whether in war or peace. I do not dispute that. But I do point out that from time to time concessions are made great industries and corporations which certainly go for beyond that point.
I agree with those who have said that as long as this war lasts we cannot emphasize the production of civilian goods, that we must continue to manufacture to the full extent of

War Appropriation-Supplies
our capacity, war material for the armed forces, and that production of civilian goods may be considered only when, all our obligations to the armed services have been met.
When I heard the Minister of Munitions and Supply the other day outlining the work of his department I was struck by the references to the enormous undertakings that Canada has engaged upon since the war began.. When we compare what we have done in these four and one-half years of war with the condition of this country in the ten years prior to the war, under both a Conservative government and a Liberal government, we are appalled to think that the country was allowed to drift into the condition in which we knew it economically during the ten dreadful years before the war broke out.
To the end of 1943, for example, we have spent on various phases of the war effort the enormous sum of $10,824 millions, or, as I may refer to it a little later, nearly 811,000 millions. This includes-and I am going to speak in round numbers-$4,000 millions for munitions, $2,750 millions for strategic materials and foodstuffs, $2,250 millions in production of material and equipment for Canada's armed forces at home and abroad, $1,500 millions in Canada for capital assistance to industry and defence construction. I take these figures as at December, 1943, from the government publication entitled "Canada at War." Almost $11,000 millions have been expended in war material, war industries, and other facilities and equipment of all kinds in connection with our war effort. Much of this has been destroyed or worn out, but many assets remain and will remain when the war ends.
As I say, although our concentration must be upon- the conduct of -the war; yet the pattern of the post-war world will be decided by what we do now. This afternoon I am going to ask what we are doing now and what is to be done when the war is over with the tremendous assets which we have built up in this country? To a very large extent, as we heard from the minister and from the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday, this will be decided by the new War Assets Corporation under order in council P.C. 9108. There is also a crown assets allocation committee consisting of interdepartmental officials and a representative of labour and of agriculture. But I understand it to be a purely advisory committee. The real power of disposal will be in the hands of this new corporation. To quote from the order in council, the actual business of the War Assets Corporation will be as follows: It is empowered to hold, manage, operate, dispose of or deal in and with any surplus crown assets consigned or transferred
to it. It will also, according to the order in council, withhold- from Canadian or world markets, for such time as 'it may decide, all or any portion of any surplus crown assets consigned or transferred to it. Further, it is empowered- to effect sales of surplus crown assets consigned or transferred to it, in such manner and upon such terms as the company may determine. When we look at the statements which have already been made by some of the persons connected with this new crown assets corporation, we realize that parliament must closely supervise its operation.
The personnel of the War Assets Corporation includes, of course, as president, Mr. J. B. Carswell, a well-known steel manufacturer of this country. As Saturday Night well said in its issue of January 29:
The business community must be gratified that Mr. Howe (Minister of Munitions and Supply) has placed the disposal o-f surplus war assets in the hands of business men and set them up in trade, not in political and official Ottawa, but in metropolitan Montreal.
In a speech before the Canadian Construction Association the president of the corporation, Mr. Carswell, made some interesting remarks which were quoted in the Financial Post of January 29 of this year. This is what he said:
Since the key job of the corporation is to protect the going economy against impingement of war surpluses, it stands to reason the corporation should never get into competition with industry-which is another [DOT]-_ of saying it should not sell direct to the consumer but rather to those whose legitimate business it is to deal with the article concerned and on a basis that, within the corporation's powers, will ensure reasonable profit to dealer and reasonable price to consumer.
Three years ago a prominent business man told a committee of this house that in his opinion at that time there should be set up a committee of business men whose duty it would be to consider ways and means of disposing of crown property and of material in such a manner as not to interfere in any way with established industry. If that policy is carried out we shall find that the War Assets Corporation, instead of being of assistance to the people of Canada, will further strengthen some of the vested industrial and financial interests in this country. I say to the minister and to the hon. member for Stormont that, because of the manner in which the government established some parts of Canada's industrial war effort, we as a nation have increased the power of some of our most powerful monopolies and cartels. I shall refer to one of them this afternoon. I shall refer to Canadian Industries Limited, the great chemical concern which is the Canadian part of the international cartel of which two of the most
War Appropriation-Supplies

powerful chemical organizations in the world, du Pont De Nemours Company and Imperial Chemical Industries Limited are the owners or the major interests.
Throughout the war the members of this group have drawn to the attention of the house and of the country the alarming growth in power of some of these powerful industrial and financial corporations, I may say quite frankly that for some months we have been making a study of Canadian Industries Limited; and while this afternoon, because of the limitations of the time at my disposal, I shall refer but briefly to the corporation, one of my colleagues, the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), will supplement what I have to say.
When the war broke out, Canadian Industries Limited, an organization which at that time had assets of some $75,000,000, established a wholly owned subsidiary company known as Defence Industries Limited, in order of course to separate entirely their war business from their civilian and ordinary commercial enterprises. Since 1939 Defence Industries Limited has directed and operated, on a management-fee basis, government-owned plant and other facilities costing some $260,000,000, so far as I can gather, judging from reports issued in this house from time to time, this capital of $260,000,000 was advanced partly on Canadian, account and partly on British account; and last year, as we know, an agreement was entered into between Great Britain and Canada, whereby this country took over the British obligations and properties.
This sum of $260,000,000 represents approximately thirty per cent of all Canadian government assistance to private industry. The total expenditure incurred to this company through the Department. of Munitions and Supply in the undertaking of Defence Industries Limited since the war, for construction, equipment and operation, has amounted, so far as I can gather, to some $600,000,000. I have said from time to time in this house that the policy of the government-and if other governments adopt the same policy, of those governments too-has strenghtened monopolistic industry and the cartels of which they form a part and will make it infinitely more difficult when this war ends to emancipate our people and the people of the world generally from the control of these great national and international organizations.

May I interrupt my hon. friend? I am sure he would wish to make it clear at this time that all the expenditure he mentions, in capital, is still the property of the crown. The assets created are the property of the crown, and the company has acted only in the capacity of manager in every case.

I was going to deal with that in a few minutes. I had a return brought down last May, which contains some interesting clauses, and I had intended to deal with that point. First of all, the concentration of war business in this company has certainly been enormous, and I may say that if similar businesses of that type had wished to enter into the supply of these materials they would have found it at least very difficult to do so. Thirty per cent of all our capital assistance has gone to this corporation, and the expenses incurred by Defence Industries Limited for all war purposes I believe amounted to $611,525,000.
When the minister interrupted me a minute ago I was about to refer to a sessional paper, No. 360, tabled in this house on May 28 of last year. This return indicated the manner in which the capital facilities paid for by the government may in part at least pass to the ownership in some cases, or in other cases to the control, of this corporation. In my opinion the optional purchasing clauses in some of these agreements have the effect of depriving the government in advance of all bargaining power, and in some instances appear to commit the government to a policy by which Canadian Industries Limited may acquire, without adequate and proper remuneration, properties paid for by the people. I say, some of the clauses in the contracts make that possible. Moreover, the contracts may have the effect-and this I regard as one of the gravest features of the whole situation- of perpetuating a monopoly which the operator of Defence Industries Limited, Canadian Industries Limited, has already acquired.
If we look at return No. 360, to which I have already referred, the contracts with Defence Industries Limited-some of them, that is, not all-are shown to contain the following clause in respect to plants engaged in the manufacturing of certain explosives and munitions of war. I quote:
The government shall give Defence Industries Limited a sixty-day option to purchase the plant or any part thereof, at a price it is willing to accept from any other party. If the offer is not accepted, the government is free to sell the same to any other party at a price not less than that offered to Defence Industries Limited.
At first glance this may appear to be fairly reasonable, but in some of these contracts there are restrictions on the use of properties, and these restrictions are of such a nature that only Defence Industries Limited would be interested in the purchase of the plant. Let me quote one of the restrictive clauses:
The plant is not to be used for production of product or other explosives, or any constituent elements thereof, for other than military purposes.

War Appropriation-Supplies
The plant is not to be used for the manufacture of the present product or of any constituent thereof except for military purposes. In other words, when the war is over the plant obviously would either be operated by Canadian Industries Limited or would have to be closed down. It should be noted that this condition is imposed on all purchasers and the restriction does not apply- I say this because I think it has some bearing in the opposite direction-to the machinery and equipment if the plant is demolished or dismantled. Other plants are bound by the same restrictive clauses. What are the effects of those clauses which have quite evidently been inserted at the request of the company? They clearly envisage the possibility of the plants as at present constituted producing commodities other than those they are now producing, perhaps civilian requirements, after the war, and they completely prevent that possibility from arising. The effect, of course, is to perpetuate the monopoly enjoyed by Canadian Industries Limited in regard to certain products.
In view of this, Mr. Chairman, I urge that parliament should take some note of the restrictive practices of the monopoly and the cartel of which Canadian Industries Limited is a part. We feel there is a grave risk that while we win the war on the battlefronts of the world we shall actually lose it to the great cartels which now embody the nazi idea and hold themselves above parliaments and governments.
Canadian Industries Limited is not a Canadian enterprise. It is jointly owned and controlled by the du Pont De Nemours company of the' United States and Imperial Chemical Industries Limited of the United Kingdom.

And others.
Mr. COLDW'ELL: Who between them hold, I understand, between eighty-five and ninety-five per cent of its share capital. The others have a very small interest in the corporation. These two companies are part of a world-wide international cartel which has divided and still divides the world into markets and concludes exclusive licensing and patent agreements. They also divide the territories of the world amongst themselves. Canada is exploited by this cartel through the jointly owned Canadian Industries Limited, just as South America is exploited by other companies which are similarly owned by the corporations I have named. It is true that politically Canada is a sovereign nation, but economically this international cartel treats her as a colonial area or a colonial possession.
The foreign capital, so far as I have been able to discover, invested in Canadian Industries Limited throughout its existence has amounted to not more than $7,000,000. An analysis of its profits and their disposition show that since 1910 dividends on capital have amounted to $75,000,000. In addition all assets in Canada exclusive of Defence Industries Limited amount to another $75,000,000. and the original foreign capital invested in the company in Canada seems to have amounted to less than $7,000,000.
Through Canadian Industries Limited this international cartel has exercised monopoly control of many vital products. They include, of course, types of ammunition, explosives, ammonia, chlorine, hydrochloric acid, sodium sulphate, carbon disulphide, caustic soda, many kinds of dyestuffs, specialized paints, lacquers and varnishes. It holds the patent for cellophane, and is, I believe,

I am not positive of this-in exclusive control of nylon production in this country. Furthermore there is a widespread belief that agreements existed with other firms that eliminated competition in certain important fertilizers before the war.
I say the monopoly has made enormous profits. To illustrate-
Did the hon. member suggest that this company holds a monopoly of the sodium sulphate industry in Canada?
No, I did not suggest quite that.
I think he did.
I said it holds the monopoly on many of those vital products, and among them I named sodium sulphate. Is that what the hon. member said?
Yes.
Yes, sodium sulphate.
We have millions of tons of it in Saskatchewan undeveloped.
We have millions of tons of the raw material undeveloped, but I am going to show these people have developed and controlled the market for it.
They could not get a monopoly on an article of that kind.

They have a monopoly on the manufacturing and refining of it. You can have all kinds of raw materials in the ground. We have large amounts of raw material, but where you have one group in control of the machinery, and particularly of the market, there you have the control of the product.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I said that this monopoly had made enormous profits. I could not illustrate it better than in this way. The holder of a $100 par value common share in 1910 now holds eighteen common shares of no par value which sell on to-day's markets for over $150 each. In addition, the holder will have received dividends in those years totalling $2,322 in respect of an investment of $100.
Recently the Department of Justice of the United States charged du Pont De Nemours Co. and Imperial Chemical Industries Limited with constituting a cartel in restraint of trade, and Canadian Industries Limited was named as a co-conspirator. This cartel, by the way, included agreements with I. G. Farbenindustrie, the German nazi-controlled chemical trust, and the Mitsui interests in Japan. However, I shall confine my remarks to the effect of this cartel on Canadian living standards.
The agreements between du Pont, Imperial Chemical Industries Limited and the jointly owned subsidiary, Canadian Industries Limt-ited, by ingenious methods eliminated competition in countless products in Canada. They provided for the exchange of patents, and for exclusive licensing arrangements; they provided that no one cartel partner should export into territory assigned to another partner; they provided for the sale of all du Pont and Imperial Chemical Industries products in Canada through Canadian Industries Limited only. No other company could handle their products. In particular Imperial Chemical Industries and du Pont have eliminated competition in strategic materials in Canada by entering into agreements with potential competitors. For example, in 1928 du Pont and Imperial Chemical Industries caused Canadian Industries Limited to enter into contracts with the Atlas Powder Company of Delaware, U.S.A., whereby Atlas was prevented from exporting explosives to Canada, or participating in the explosive business in Canada. That is one example. Another example is that in 1936 du Pont and Imperial Chemical Industries Limited caused Canadian Industries Limited to enter into an agreement with the National Lead Company of the United States in order to eliminate competition in titanium pigments in Canada. This agreement provided for the setting up of a new company, Canadian Titanium Pigments Limited.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
I would prefer to make my speech; then the hon. member could ask questions.
What is his authority for that statement?

I am quoting directly from a report tabled, in this particular instance, in Washington, by the committee which inquired into the chemical industry. Du Pont de Nemours Co. and Imperial Chemicals Limited are part of the cartel of which Canadian Industries Limited is a part and a subsidiary.

Let me add this, in case someone should question what a cartel is. Some people seem to imagine that agreements between governments in connection with raw materials and food supplies are in the nature of cartels. A few days ago I looked up a number of definitions, and I could find nothing to substantiate that point of view. I did. however, copy from the Encyclopaedia of Social Sciences, a standard work not only in North America but in the English-speaking world, these definitions:
The term cartel designates an association based upon a contractual agreement between enterprises in the same field of business which, while retaining their legal independence, associate themselves with a view to exerting a monopolistic influence upon the market. . . .
Cartels may be divided into three basic types, according to methods by which they exert their influence upon the market. There are cartels whose direct object is price-fixing, cartels which aim at limitation of production or supply, cartels which operate through division of territory. . . .
In general, only associations oif the larger, independent enterprises are designated as cartels.
To-day the world is faced with a revival of some of these great international cartels. They are not dead; they are only sleeping. This organization had the very closest contacts with the German chemical industry. Indeed, if one went into the whole cartel set-up-and I have not the time this afternoon to do it-of its history, he would find that before and during the last war, while apparently it slept, and in the days of peace, I believe right up to the present time, the cartel's assets were carried by these organizations as assets on the right side of the ledger. They will be ready to act when the war ends because of their control of patents and other assets.
My time is up, but I should like to add just a word. We in this house ought to take action regarding the problem of patents. Through the control of patents some of these great international cartels have built up monopolies and have thwarted the progress of industry and the safety of our people. The time is long past when we should have tackled this problem, and the last thing parliament should have done is what I believe it has done, namely, strengthened the power of monopolies and cartels in the midst of the present war emergency.

That is the basic difficulty. On, top of that, of course, is the conversion cost. While the conversion cost may be cut, I would point out that if wheat at the distillery costs $1.40 a bushel, we have a basic cost of seventy cents for a gallon of alcohol. That is fixed and unchangeable, as far as I can find out, and on top of that, of course, is the cost of conversion. I said that if wheat cost $1.40 a bushel at the distillery, that in itself would mean seventy cents a gallon for the alcohol. It actually costs ninety cents; therefore there is a conversion charge of around twenty cents a gallon involved. Perhaps by better methods that could be cut tc ten cents a gallon, but my hon. friend will appreciate that even then the cost of alcohol from wheat is vastly greater than the cost of alcohol from petroleum products. Now, what about the quality of the product?

Before the
minister leaves that point may I ask him a question? As I understood the minister, he gave a figure for making alcohol from wheat and from petroleum products. Would he have the figures as to what the final rubber costs are from wheat and from petroleum products?
War Appropriation-Supplies

I shall trace that through if my hon. friend wishes. I cannot give him the costs of butadiene because I have not them at my finger-tips. The costs of butadiene, which is one of the two basic products of rubber is about one-third of the cost of butadiene made from wheat alcohol. I may say that wheat is not used in the United States. Com is the base there, if it is available. It makes a cheaper alcohol. Ordinarily a still cheaper alcohol can be made from molasses. Alcohol is alcohol and butadiene is butadiene. It does not make any difference what you make butadiene from. Butadiene is a chemical, and when it has the same degree of purity it is exactly the same regardless of the source of the manufacture.

I understand
that at. Sarnia they made synthetic rubber from wheat in the early stages. I wondered if the minister had the figures with him.

Yes, they made it from
alcohol, but in starting up a plant it is very difficult to get costs that mean very much. Rubber made at Sarnia to-day is slightly below the cost of the imported rubber. The import price of rubber is about forty-one cents a pound. According to the last report I received, our costs are running around forty cents a pound to-day; but they are dropping very rapidly and we expect within a matter of weeks to get down to a cost of approximately twenty cents a pound. We hope ultimately to arrive at a cost of around sixteen to seventeen cents a pound.

That is less
than the price of raw rubber before the war?

Yes, and much less than raw rubber to-day. The average price of raw rubber .before the war was roughly fifteen cents a pound. Frequently it went as high as twenty-five cents a pound. Of course, that is rubber at the seaboard. We expect our rubber to compete freely with natural rubber and perhaps have a price advantage, if we can read the cost of rubber from the past as the cost of rubber in the future.
As I say, one ingredient of rubber is butadiene. The other is styrene. We make both products on the same property. We make butadiene at our Sarnia plant; on the same property we make our styrene, and on the same property we combine the two together into rubber through a process known as polymerization. In that we used a certain amount of dandelion. As my hon. friend may know, through the Department of Agriculture we encouraged the planting of dandelions for

that purpose at about the time that we started the synthetic rubber plant, and we are using dandelions in our process to-day. Unfortunately we have not enough to be much of a factor, but the use of dandelions is helpful in the polymerization process. It is said to help the process of converting the basic materials into the finished rubber. However, I do not think anyone has made rubber wholly from dandelions commercially. I asked our experts what the costs would be and they estimated about $10 a pound. They admitted it could be done, but they said that the cost of making rubber from dandelions alone would amount to about $10 a pound in the finished product, which, of course, puts it out of the way as a commercially feasible process.
What about milkweed?

From the point of view of use in making rubber the two products are very much the same. I may say that we are having some difficulty in getting our farmers to cultivate milkweed. We paid them for their crop and I think they found it was not a very attractive element in farming. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture can give more data on that than I can from the point of view of milkweed and dandelions as a crop.
As to the quality of the rubber, I think our rubber is as good as any made on this continent, and perhaps as good as any made anywhere. It is recognized everywhere as a first-class grade of synthetic rubber. The difficulty we are having in manufacturing tires is that of processing the rubber that we have. I suppose it took ten or twelve years for the industry to make, from natural rubber, the tires that were being sold just before the war. As many of us will remember, the tires we used to buy ten years ago were guaranteed for perhaps only 1,000 or 2,000 miles, but just before the war we expected a tire to last for 20,000 or 25,000 miles.
We have been going through that process with tires made from synthetic rubber. Great strides have been made. I said in my report that to-day tires could be guaranteed as eighty per cent as good, as respects wearing qualities, as tires made from crude rubber. That is a marked advance in only a matter of months. Perhaps I was a little conservative in my statement as it would apply to the type of tires used on ordinary passenger cars. Many of our tests show that the same mileage can be obtained from that type of tire, using synthetic rubber, as can be obtained from the same tire built of natural rubber.

War Appropriation-Supplies
The difficulty is in connection with the heavy-duty tire the big truck tire and particularly those very large tires used in connection with mobile artillery.
How do costs compare?

I shall talk about quality first. The difficulty is that for the early tires built, it was found that in driving at high speed and with heavy loads, the tires heated, and deteriorated through the action of the heat on the rubber. Even to-day, we are using about twenty per cent natural rubber in the biggest artillery tires, and only eighty per cent synthetic rubber.
That is, virgin rubber.
Twenty per cent natural rubber, and eighty per cent synthetic.
Not reclaimed rubber?

No; reclaimed is not used in tires at all. Tires, however, have been greatly improved. The natural rubber tire used cotton fabric, but to-day in the heavy-duty synthetic tire we are using a celanese fabric which is stronger than cotton, and permits us to carry the same loads with thinner tires. This has the effect of reducing heating.
So that I believe it can be said that we are well on the road to having a satisfactory solution of our rubber problem. I have never undertaken a war project which has caused me as much worry and concern as did that of synthetic rubber. At the time we undertook the project, no synthetic rubber had been made on this continent, outside of laboratories. We were very much in the dark as to costs, and we were not at all sure that sufficient engineering data was available to allow us to work out the process. I went to rtiy colleagues and asked for an appropriation of $45,000,000 to undertake this project. I had to point out that our stock-pile of crude rubber at that time could last for only a matter of months, that the chances of getting more were not good, and that the world stock-pile of rubber would run out in a matter of months. I put it to them as a race against time, with the possibility of disaster if the project did not turn out well.
The plant is now completed, and getting close to full operation. We have had no serious disappointments in connection with it. Even though it was rushed through in winter months, the cost was within ten per cent of the estimate I placed before my colleagues. It was brought in pretty much at the estimated time, and the product is first class. It happens that ours is the only wholly integrated rubber plant built on this
continent, where all the products are made, and the rubber completed, on the same lot. That has had the effect of cutting down our costs and, from a comparison of data supplied by officers in charge of operations in the United States, I find that our costs are favourable. I believe we have a splendid industry and, for the chemists, a tremendously interesting one. At some stage in the process, simply by turning a petcock one can draw off almost every element of petroleum. The various elements of petroleum are the basic substances from which a great variety of products is made. I believe that not only will this plant continue in the future to make rubber, but it will be the centre of a great industry and1 the source of the production of a great variety of other products.
I believe it has been perhaps the most interesting project of the war, and one which will make a contribution to Canada's future industrial progress as great as that of any we have undertaken. I would hope that any hon. member who finds himself in the vicinity of Sarnia would take the opportunity ol visiting the plant. I am sure he would find it an interesting and inspiring experience.

What factories have been closed down as result of the cancellation of agreements, and what has been done with the employees of those factories?
I come now to the general position in regard to controls and controllers. The minister dealt

with the production of instruments and communication equipment, and, as reported on page 1693 of Hansard, he said:

The preamble of P.C. 1980 with reference to this company states:
The Sutton-Horsley Company Limited, which operates a plant in the city of Toronto, is engaged in the manufacture of special types of aircraft parts and accessories required for use in the production of aircraft for His Majesty.

If my information is correct the conditions at this plant have not been any too good since the controller was appointed. I understand that the number of employees has decreased from 1,200 to less than 400 and that lay-offs are continuing from day to day. A rumour is being circulated that the place is to be closed down within a period of time. What is the situation with regard to the Sutton-Horsley Company? Why has there been this reduction in the number of employees? Has the production of this plant increased or decreased since March, 1943? What course does the government in-

tend to take in order to ensure production of these articles which are so necessary in connection with our aircraft production?
I pass now to another matter dealt with by the minister, the production of wood fuel, and I intend to submit an example of what I consider gross inefficiency on the part of those in charge. The minister dealt with this matter on page 1702 of Hansard, when he said:
Wood fuel control was established to stimulate production, and to supervise the distribution of wood, in order that there might be no hardship during the present winter.
And again:
In addition to the production subsidy, transportation subsidies have also been paid, in order to facilitate the movement of wood to probable distressed areas. The wood fuel controller^ also initiated a number of special cutting projects, as a means of building up government-owned banks of wood fuel, which could be held in reserve and shipped to any areas where distress was imminent.
I ask the minister to explain this set-up. I know the circumstances under which wood fuel control was established. I am going to give one example and then I shall ask the minister to explain the whole position, giving the number of camps established, the results that flowed therefrom and the cost of producing the wood fuel in each area.
I deal now with the situation particularly at the head of the lakes. There, after the appointment of a controller, plans were proceeded with for taking out 75,000 cords of fuel wood. Directives were given to those who were to take out this wood, and ceiling prices were established. There was a ceiling price- at the lakes, a different ceiling price at Winnipeg, and further west still another ceiling price. The government, through the controller, directed these firms at the head of the lakes to get out fuel wood, the prices paid to the -operators being as follows: for poplar, $7.50; pine, $8.25; tamarack and birch, $10.50. Strangely enough, the Manitoba ceiling price for the same wood, including the one dollar subsidy, was $5.50 for poplar, $6.25 for pine and $7.25 for tamarack.
The freight rate on this wood to the city of Winnipeg was from sixteen to twenty-one cents per 100 pounds. This wood could not be used until it was reasonably dry. A cord of green poplar weighs 5,400 pounds and, when dry, about 2,500 pounds. A cord of birch weighs 5,000 to 6,000 pounds when green, and about half that when it is dried out.
Winnipeg had sufficient fuel. In the province of Manitoba fuel was available at a shipping rate of 4j to 7 cents per 100 pounds. But what happened a few weeks ago? An order came from the controller that wood

shall be taken from the head of the lakes production. So what did they do? They shipped the wood to Winnipeg. I have given the initial price of the wood. Take poplar, for hfttance. 'They did not wait to ship it until it was dry in order to save freight rates. The wood was not needed in Winnipeg and it could have been kept in a stock-pile at the head of the lakes until it could be used. The fuel dealers of Winnipeg informed the controller that there was no market there for the wood. But that did not matter. The wood had to be sold in Winnipeg. Poplar cost S7.50 a cord to produce, and they shipped it to Winnipeg and paid an $8 freight rate. It cost $15.50 a cord to produce and deliver in Winnipeg. That does not take into account administrative costs, and then the government sold it in Winnipeg at $5.15 a cord.

Does my hon. friend recall the day when a motion was made to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of great public emergency, when we were told that the people of the country would freeze for lack of fuel? May I tell him that this last winter no one in Canada went cold for lack of fuel. Does he think that just the usual means were required to overcome this great national emergency which was painted by his party, or is his party in the habit of moving to adjourn the house in a great national emergency when there is no emergency at all?
I do not criticize the minister for getting the wood out.
Thank God for that.

But I do not thank the Deity that this wood was shipped to Winnipeg, paying an SS freight rate, when it could have been stored at the head of the lakes until needed. That is why I criticize the government. If they had left the wood at the head of the lakes, all that it would have cost would have been $7.50 stored, until it was needed and was dry. Instead of so much moisture being hauled to Winnipeg, the wood could have been left at the head of the lakes until it was needed.

It seemed important to my hon. friend, when lie moved to adjourn the house, that there be enough wood to keep the people from freezing. A lot of the wood was left at the head of the lakes, but we shipped a fair amount to Winnipeg in case the weather turned cold. We are not judges of the weather; we cannot tell what the weather will be next month. Let him remember that, and let him tell me how much surplus fuel there is in Winnipeg to-day. He is the greatest second guesser in the house.

After all, when the minister speaks I listen to him, and he can answer me afterwards, as I do him. Just because the minister realizes that $800,000 or thereabouts was thrown away, naturally he becomes annoyed. He was warned about this, and his controller was warned that the wood was not needed in Winnipeg, that wood could have been obtained in Manitoba at a freight rate at 4| to 7 cents. But the order of the controller to the people of Winnipeg was: You have to take 12,500 cords from the head of the lakes, regardless of your wishes or your needs. I do not criticize the government or the minister for any efforts that were made to get out the wood. But the department had it stored at the head of the lakes, and it was not needed in Winnipeg at that time. The freight rate to Winnipeg would have been just exactly one-half if the wood had been left until dry in the stock-pile at the head of the lakes to meet emergencies. But for some reason best known to the controller, and acting against the advice of those he consulted with, against the advice he received from those with whom he came in contact in the trade, he went ahead as controllers sometimes do, regardless of the treasury of Canada, and in that one small item the people of Canada have lost a matter of from $600,000 to $900,000.

The minister's statement, in which he reviewed his department, and his reply to the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) earlier in the day, indicate, I think, certain things:	First of all, the
extent to which we were industrially unpre-pared'for this war, as we were unprepared in the military sense; second, the extent to which the minister, as he claimed, was forced to take the enterprises that were at hand, the organizations that were at hand, in order to get the job done. It appears quite evident that he was pretty much at the mercy of enterprise as it was organized in the country. I think his speech also indicates the extent to which private industry in this country had failed to meet the demands of war and how necessary it became for the government to come to the assistance of private industry in that endeavour.
We learn that the government had to come to the assistance of enterprise to the extent now of somewhere about 8900,000,000 of capital investment; that the planning of production that was needed had to be done by the government, and that priorities and controls were established by the government and crown companies were set up. Numerous private enterprises which had failed to deliver the goods were of necessity placed under government ownership in order to do the greatest production job that this country has ever undertaken. I wish to say at this point that those hon. gentlemen in this chamber who place their faith so unequivocally in private enterprise, who still believe that private enterprise is responsible for the production of war essentials and who want to depend so exclusively on private enterprise for our post-war reconstruction, would do well to consider the part that the government has been called upon to play in our war effort .
There are those in this committee who have been quite loud in their protestations about our lack of military preparedness when the war began, and who have been loud in adopting the attitude of "I told you so," and accusing others of being responsible for that lack of preparation. These same hon. gentlemen have been silent regarding the industrial handicaps that we suffered and slow to observe that many of those handicaps were deliberately imposed upon the country by privately owned monopolies and cartels. Only now are we beginning to learn the extent to which Germany had succeeded in the pre-war days in her twofold policy of arming herself and disarming the democracies. Germany's war preparation was just as effective in the field of science and industry as it was in the field of military preparation. Through her international cartels and agreements, her monopoly and restrictions on the use of patents, she was able to restrict the production of many essentials of the democracies to a point that required many years to overtake. Only by
War Appropriation-Supplies

an examination of our situation and its causes at the outbreak of the war, the hamstringing of our war effort, can we plan for our future security or learn how to avoid world war number three.
Almost every shortage that has impeded our war effort can be attributed to a cartel. When men died of malaria in Bataan it was for lack of quinine made unavailable because of the cartel which administered the affairs of the producers of that product.
AVhen we tried to expand our factories and needed tools we were hamstrung by agreements which had been made between Carboloy Incorporated and Krupps. When we needed cobalt for its hardening qualities of steel in order to make our machine tools we found the Canadian field comparatively undeveloped because of international agreements and cartels. When scientific instruments were scarce and optical instruments were not to be found, and civilians were asked to volunteer their binoculars and high-powered cameras, it was because of agreements signed in 1921 for a term of twenty-one years between Bausch and Lomb of the United States and the Zeiss interests of Germany. When we were desperately in need of tin we found a shortage on account of similar tactics by the British-controlled cartel, the international tin committee. Just how far these huge corporations, enjoying the protection and freedom of our institutions and the legal protection which they enjoy under our patent laws, will be permitted to continue to exercise treaty-making powers in our essential commodities and strategic materials without supervision by the government and responsibility to governmental authority, will be one of the principal questions that we shall have to decide in all our post-war planning.
This afternoon the minister denied any association of his department with Canadian Industries Limited, a member, as the leader of this group has already shown, of an international cartel. I think in making his statement the minister must have had in mind his department's dealing with the matter of explosives; for I cannot think that this company which operates fifteen important divisions and on its own account supplies essential material for forty-five distinct war uses, has had no dealings with the government. I cannot think that company has had no dealings with the government through the minister's department.
I wish to deal with the question of the plant at Nobel, but before doing so I should like to give a brief resume of some of the activities of the parent company of Defence Industries Limited. Canadian Industries Limited, the

company that is the sole owner of Defence Industries Limited. Canadian Industries Limited, as was pointed out this afternoon, is in its turn almost completely owned by du Pont and Imperial Chemical Industries, the first of the United States, and the second of Great Britain. This company was organized first in 1910 as Canadian Explosives Limited. It was organized by du Pont and Imperial Chemical Industries for the purpose of buying controlling interests in five or six small Canadian companies in which they were interested, five or six companies at that time engaged in the production of explosives. The company flourished during the first great war. The minister went to great pains to show that no great profits were made or that no one has yet shown that great profits, or profiteering, as he called it, has been shown by those engaged in the explosives industry during this war. I think we can say for his benefit that so far there has been no evidence of any profiteering on the same scale as that which took place during the last great war. This particular company, Canadian Industries Limited, flourished during the last war. In 1917 it paid on its invested capital dividends of 256 per cent. In 1918 its stockholders received a dividend of 56 per cent, plus 100 per cent stock dividend. In 1920 another 50 per cent stock dividend was paid to its shareholders. Probably not until somebody is capable of bringing to the light of day the hidden costs and the real profits that will be made in this war shall we know really to what extent profiteering has been going on.
In 1927 this company changed its name to Canadian Industries Limited. Shareholders were given six shares in the new company for each one in the old. So that when we estimate the profits which this company has made in this war, these profits must be multiplied by eighteen, if you are to relate those profits to the original capital investment; because the holders of the original stocks now hold eighteen shares for every one of their original holdings. Since the beginning of this war the net profits per share on the common stock of this company have ranged from S7.50 in 1919 down to $5.25 a share in 1943. This is quite a different picture from that of 1917, 1918 and 1919.
Already the statement' has been made that this particular company, like other cartels, is above the regulations and laws of the country in which it operates, and that this particular company, through its agreement with du Pont and its other parent company, has restricted again and again both imports into and exports out of this country.
I have quite a few examples, and shall mention again one or two already mentioned. In
