1928 Canadian Industries Limited attempted to export a new waterproof finish for shot shells to the United States. Du Pont, one of the parent companies, prevented this, and later took the patents of the new process for itself. In 1929 Imperial Chemicals and du Pont prohibited Canadian Industries Limited from exporting to the West Indies. At that time the Canadian government was subsidizing the steamship companies for transportation to the West Indies, and was anxious to increase our export.
There is a letter in existence from an officer of Canadian Industries Limited, written in 1939, in which he said he felt that the position of Canadian Industries Limited with its government would be strengthened if his company were free to quote on certain products in the West Indies, while at the same time protecting Imperial Chemical's prices, since the refusal to quote had led to complaints to	the
government.
Again in 1930 du Pont prevented this Canadian, or so-called Canadian Company, from selling finishes of the duco type for shipment to South America. In 1932 and 1934 du Pont prevented this Canadian company from exporting a product known as pontan, a coated textile product, because it would conflict with the parent company's product in Great Britain.
The story regarding imports is similar. In 1928 du Pont and Imperial Chemicals caused Canadian Industries Limited to enter into a contract with the Atlas Powder Company, and this is one of the reasons why, when war came, the explosives industry in this country was a monopoly in the hands of Canadian Industries Limited. Another United States company which had sought to export its products to this country was prevented from doing so by a contract under which it agreed not to export explosives to Canada, or to participate in any such business in Canada, leaving Canadian Industries Limited a clear field.
Prior to 1936 du Pont, Imperial Chemical Industries and Canadian Industries Limited, in order to eliminate competition between themselves and the Shawinigan Chemical Company entered into a contract with the Shawinigan company which provided that Shawinigan would restrict its activities in the chemical field to products made from acetylene, and that Canadian Industries Limited would refrain from manufacturing such products. Then, in 1936 a similar arrangement was made with the International Paper Company, which prevented the latter from entering the manufacturing of chemical products, and prevented Canadian Industries Limited from entering pulp and paper production.
In 1936 a similar arrangement was made with Courtaulds Limited whereby Canadian Industries Limited agreed to refrain from manufacturing rayons and Courtaulds from manufacturing chemical products in Canada. Similarly in 1939 Canadian Industries Limited and the Sauffer Chemical Company of California organized the Cornwall Chemical Company, to be the sole manufacturer of carbon disulphide in Canada, so that all competition in this commodity in Canada could be eliminated. I quote these as examples of monopoly and cartel control, in restricting both import and export trades into and out of this country respectively.

Defence Industries Limited is to make an offer if it desires to purchase the plant or any part thereof. I find that restrictive clause in some of the contracts or agreements with Defence Industries Limited. It looks very much to me as though this company, because of its strategic position in this particular field, was able to extract from the government terms and conditions in the agreement which in effect will leave the government very little choice, when the war ends, except to demolish or remove those plants. That, of course, is a convenient arrangement for C.I.L. It leaves them entirely free to expand their peace-time production, and they have expanded enormously during the war. They can scrap the D.I.L. plants; their peace-time plants remain intact. They have no commitments; they have no plant; they have no expansions such as have been made for war purposes to worry about when the war is over, and of course they have no funded debt.
As I stated earlier, one of the great problems of any government that seeks to achieve maximum production when the war is over, or to use the productive enterprises of this country, will be the existence of these monopoly enterprises in this country, many of them with international interlocking directorates and cartel arrangements; and these monopolies will be emerging from this war-* let us make no mistake about it-much more strongly entrenched than they were at the beginning of the war. The ineffectiveness of legislation or legislative c>
ntrol has been demonstrated, I think, in the United States. We find that notwithstanding our Combines Investigation Act, notwithstanding the glaring revelations before our price spreads committee some years ago, notwithstanding certain prosecutions which have taken place under the Combines Investigation Act, no effective control has yet been applied to these concerns. Hon. gentlemen may disagree with our plans or our policies for dealing with these concerns; but let me say that the future of any political body in this house-any political party, whether it be Liberal, Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or anything else- is not of paramount concern to this country. The future of Canada is the thing that is of paramount concern to this country, and whatever party seeks to govern this country when the war is over must face this question of Cartels and cartel agreements, and must find some way of making these enterprises serve the interests of the common people.

rather hurriedly, I will say that. But, as a matter of fact, what I am contending is true, that we have not had anything in relation to our strategic position as part of this dominion qua the other side, where all the stuff had to be shipped and where large savings in transportation facilities could have been made. Chicken feed is right.
Then, let us go to the table on mechanical transport. Well, we did not have any factories equipped for mechanical transport, and we could hardly expect to get any of the $10,000, 000 that were expended under that table. I am not making any particular complaint about that. Then I come along to the table on tanks and armoured vehicles. This was all new work and I assume that it required big plants and a lot of expense, but we did not get any of that. No crown plants were built. No crown companies were operated. No crown plants were operated by the government, but there were crown plants operated by private enterprise and I suggest that we might have got a share of that. Then there were privately owned and operated plants. The total expenditure under that heading was $9,444,000, but nothing was spent in the maritime provinces.
I come now to signals, communications and instruments on page 12, table 1A-9. Total expenditure under that heading was $12,569,900 and not a cent spent in the maritimes. The bulk of that, of course, was Research Enterprises Limited, and, that had to be located near Ottawa somewhere. It would be unthinkable to put that down in the province of New Brunswick. That sort of thing just is not done.
Then we come to machine tools and gauges. A large number of more or less small companies participated in the government largess. The total expenditure was $5,050,427, and not a cent went to the maritimes. I do not understand why that work could not have been

done down there. It is said that the people down there did not have initiative. The people down there never had a chance to show initiative. They never were encouraged to show initiative.
The national policy.

That is the policy. I am glad the hon. member for Lunenburg agrees with me that it is true, because he operates a machine shop himself. That ought to hold him for a while.
Then there is table 1A-11, general purchasing and miscellaneous, purchases of merchandise. Crown plants government operated, nil; crown companies government operated, nil; crown plants operated by private corporations, $5,000; privately owned and operated plants, general merchandising; Trenton Steel Works is the only one and it received $23,268 out of a total of $530,972,648.
Then I come to section B, aircraft manufacturing. I have failed to find anything that is specifically allocated to the maritime provinces except it may be the Canadian Car and Foundry Company Limited at Amherst, and I am not at all sure that any part of this sum was spent in the maritimes, although I am willing to assume that some portion, perhaps a substantial portion of the $4,144,000, was spent there, but outside of that there is no evidence of any part of the total of $53,000,000 odd spent in the maritime provinces.
Then there is aircraft overhaul and repair. There is a total of $13,82S,833, and again I fail to find the names of any maritime province concerns except possibly it may be Canadian Car and Foundry which, I believe, operates a plant or does some repair work at its Amherst plant.
Then we have Clark-Ruse. I want to call attention to this about Clark-Ruse. They operate a plant over in Dartmouth. I was there the other day and I want the country to listen to this. They have seven or eight hundred employees.

From when? These men are still working there. A notice was put up that after a certain date-

Absolutely; I saw the notice.
I will take the minister's word.
Why make the statement?
Where are they to be placed?
Two thousand men are required in the same city for a similar class of work in the shipyard there.
For aircraft repairs?
No. We repair aircraft when they are damaged, and when they are not damaged we have no repairs.
I am not questioning the fact.
Then why are you-
I wonder what the minister is going to do with them. I suppose he will fall back-
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that this helps the employees in their-

No; I
imagine that is probabty true. Five hundred men are going to lose their jobs and I ask the minister what is to become of them. I suppose he will fall back on the usual stereotyped answer that national selective service will look after them. I wish to tell him something about national selective service as told to me by an employer of labour going down on the train the other night. The government knows; I do not know whether it is the minister's department.
It is a smoking-car story, I take it?
No; it is right from the horse's mouth. The minister can take it from me, it is Simon-pure, and right out of the horse's mouth.
It took place on the train; I presumed it was a smoking-car story.

And that is a respectable place to talk about things; at least I hope so. This is about the Pennfield airport. We have heard something aboqt the Pennfield airport; the hon. member for Charlotte knows something about it. The Pennfield airport was condemned by the Department of Transport. I was glad to see it built. I thought it was a proper place to have an airport. However its fortunes have been varied. Schools have been moved in and schools have been moved out. And we had it among the list of twenty-eight schools that were being closed down the other day,

the operational school at Pennfield airport.
I do not know what they are going to do with the airport, but I will tell you what the government is doing. They have doubled the capacities of the runways, at a cost of $500,000, and the work is still going on. I should like the minister to explain what use they intend to make out of that airport when they have spent this additional amount of money in doubling the surface of the airport.
But that is not the point I wish to make. The contractor wanted a hundred men. He applied to national selective service in Saint John. He got fifteen men in two months- and only six of them stayed.
You are not blaming the Minister of Munitions and Supply for that?

No; I am just passing out a bouquet to national selective service. They got fifteen men in two months, and six of them stuck. When the contractor complained they said they could not get them. Then they said to the contractor, "Can you?" "Yes", he said, "I can get them." And he got them. They said, "Go ahead and get them and report the names to us, and we will put them through as if we had got them." That is the wonderful performance of national selective service. They confessed their inability to get them, but the private enterprise got them.
Let us get back to the maritimes.

You bet. Then, Clark-Ruse has had an advance of about two and a half million dollars. I should like to ask the minister is that is recoverable, nr if it is a dead loss. I would ask if that plant is closed down because of lack of work, and what is to become of it.
My hon. friend has been complaining about no plants built in the maritimes. Now he has a very decent industry that has done a fine job and he asks if the money is recoverable.
I have asked if that money is recoverable.
Those buildings are owned by the crown.
What are they going to be used for, if the work is to be closed down?
If the maritimes keep yapping about them-
"Yapping"?-I resent that.
Yes, yapping; that is all.

I never yap at anything. The minister is doing all the yapping now. And I say, too, that that is a very rude statement and he ought to take it back. If he is a gentleman he will take it back-and I know he is a gentleman, and I know he will take it back.
I now come to table IB-3, at page 17, and turn to the heading "Aircraft miscellaneous", and notice that there has been some contribution by maritime provinces in shipbuilding. I turn particularly to part I, section C, table 1C-1, which refers specifically to naval shipbuilding, and shows an expenditure of $1,186,918 in connection with crown plants, government-operated. In the list there is the Princess Louise berth, wherever that is. Then under the heading "crown companies, government operated", we find Quebec Shipyards Limited and Toronto Shipbuilding Company Limited. Someone else can deal with the Toronto Shipbuilding Company. I understand the minister is not too proud of it.
Part of that is in the province of New Brunswick.

I would not think so. They had a little assembling plant at Indian Town. They brought them down, put them together and shipped them overseas, when they might have done a lot of things there.
I come now to privately owned and operated plants, and- I find the Halifax Shipyards Limited got $579,160. Then there is another item for J. D. Irving Company Limited which, I suppose, was in connection with the landing barge programme, and they did not take up any amount. Of the $9,731,888 in connection with this table for naval shipbuilding, the maritime provinces got only a little over half a million.
We come now to cargo shipbuilding, and I call the minister's attention to table 1C-2 at page 19. Under this heading I find the Pictou berth, with a commitment of $388,300, and an expenditure of $301,054. I understand that that was for the building of a wharf at Pictou harbour. Was it done by the Fundy Construction company. I Wonder if that has a familiar ring to the ears of any hon. members from the province of Nova Scotia. They will tell us who the Fundy Construction company is. They were paid a little over 8140,000 for the work they did on that wharf, and then the wharf slid into the harbour.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member who has just taken his seat has considerable justification for the remarks he has made in connection with the allocating of war industries. But I do not think he has as much cause for complaint as those of us who come from Saskatchewan, because we have received absolutely nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He said that when he started.
I started complaining over three years ago about that, and-
Would my hon. friend let me make a comment?
Yes.
The greatest proportional increase in industrial activity in the Dominion of Canada during war time has taken place in Saskatchewan. Let him think that over.
If there was nothing before, and you spend a dollar, what is the percentage of that?

The minister knows that as far as our province is concerned it is still practically nil. However, I made my complaints and offered suggestions a number of years ago in connection with this matter, and I realize that we are now at a stage of the war where there is no particular use in dwelling upon things unless you think there is a possibility you may be able to get somewhere. I believe any hon. member from Saskatchewan, no matter from what party he might come, would be willing to put forth an effort if he thought he could obtain results.
The matter I should like to raise is in connection with synthetic rubber. Last year I spoke at some length in connection with this matter and made special reference to the production of rubber from surplus agricultural products. At that time the minister informed us that after due consideration it had been determined that the best process to produce rubber was by the use of petroleum. He

stated that they had embarked on the programme and were going to see it through. At the same time he held out some hope that possibly in the future, if circumstances warranted, investigations might be continued into the production of alcohol from agricultural products. Last year the minister stated that the process they were using to produce synthetic rubber from petroleum had been obtained from the United States. He is reported at page 3700 of Hansard of June 16, 1943, as follows:
Extensive development work in the processes involved in the production of butadiene from a petroleum base had been made in the United States, and Canada was offered the use of all information obtained on the same basis as similar projects in the United States.
And on page 3701:
The problems of developing organizations to produce synthetic rubber in satisfactory amounts and qualities and of procuring or training the necessary operating personnel for the various plants in the Canadian project could, for obvious reasons, best be met and solved by following the main lines of the United States programme.
He went on to state that even though they had embarked on that programme it did not necessarily preclude the use of industrial alcohol made from agricultural products. If, as the minister stated the other day, this programme is a complete success, if it is the most economical means of producing synthetic rubber, then. I and those of us who come from western Canada will have to be content for the time being. There are one or two points, however, I should like to draw to the attention of the administration before I ask one or two questions in connection with the operations of the plant at Sarnia.
As far as the use of surplus agricultural products are concerned, it is not so much a question of the cost per bushel of the wheat or the cost per unit of the agricultural product involved; it is more that we on the prairies felt that, because our agricultural production was so great that at times we produced more than could be used in Canada for food purposes or exported for the same purposes, therefore some of this production should be used in the manufacture of synthetic rubber. Last year the minister stated that the plant at Sarnia would be in full porduction by November. He stated also that they would be making in this plant 37,000 tons of buna-S rubber and 8,000 tons of butyl rubber when they were in full production. The plant was to be in full production by November of last year, but the other day the minister stated, as reported on page 1705 of Hansard, that it would not be in full production until May of

War Appropriation-Supplies
this year, as far as the buna-S plant was concerned, and until July, as far as the butyl plant was concerned.
I think the committee is entitled to an explanation for that delay. It is true it is only a matter of months, but there must have been some bottle-necks or mistakes encountered by those in charge of production, and possibly these might be worth following up in order that similar mistakes might be corrected in the future.- The minister stated last year that the production of butyl rubber, which I understand is used for inner tubes, was to be 9,000 tons, but he now states that they are obtaining only 150 tons per month, or 1,800 tons a year. In other words, in order to meet that figure the increase in production between now and next July will have to be over fourfold.
My attention has been directed to certain newspaper and' magazine reports in the United States to the effect that the synthetic rubber programme on this continent has not been quite as successful as those who devised the plants thought it would be. If the plant in this country is such a success and they .are going on without much difficulty, perhaps the minister will explain why the United States, with whom we are collaborating, have not taken advantage of the wisdom which was apparently used by the Canadian authorities to obtain such a success in their programme? I was interested in reading in Time of February 14 of this year an article on rubber, where it is stated that they are using more alcohol to produce synthetic rubber than they anticipated using, whereas the petroleum end of it was bogging down. I should like to quote from page 33 of this magazine as follows:
When "Bull Bill" Jeffers bowed out of Washington as rubber czar last September, he flatly announced: "The big job is done." In the long months that followed, optimism flowed from the rubber director's office; full-page, breast-beating advertisements of many an oil company happily assured the United States that the battle of rubber had been won. But last week, a sheaf of ominous straws fluttered out of Washington:
The allotment of synthetic rubber previously scheduled for civilian tires in the next five months has been halved.
OP A drastically screwed dowm tire rationing, shifted the rationing basis from mileage to essential occupations.
Rubber boss Bradley Dewey slapped a ban on the use of synthetic rubber in many a civilian item, even nipped plans for girdle manufacture.
And further on:
Out of alcohol. The famed Baruch rubber report handed oilmen the big job of butadiene production for buna-S (75 per cent butadiene plus 25 per cent styrene equals buna-S). Oilmen were to turn out 65 per cent of all United
States butadiene production. The remainder was to come from the alcohol process, which was loudly damned as a farm-bloc plot to use up surplus grain.
But by last week the alcohol process was the brightest spot in the picture. Paced by Carbide and Carbon's plants at Institute, West Virginia, and Louiseville, Kentucky, butadiene from alcohol is now actually furnishing 75 per cent of all butadiene. Built last year to produce only 220,000 tons, the plants have been geared up to 150 per cent of capacity, and can turn out an unbelievable 330,000 tons a year. Thus, the alcohol process has shouldered in to take over the big job. Even by the end of the year, when all petroleum butadiene plants will presumably be in production, alcohol will still furnish half the butadiene.
The article goes on to refer to the difficulty of obtaining enough grain to produce the alcohol, and I understand from what I have seen in the press that they are importing grain from this country for the purpose and also importing industrial alcohol. The article goes on to say:
But Rubber Boss Dewey calmly points to the glowing alcohol-production record to prove that the programme was right, the oilmen wrong. The hard fact is that the much simpler alcohol process ran into fewer production kinks than those which knotted up petroleum butadiene production, split as it is among 13 companies, tinkering with five different processes. What worked like a dream in the laboratory is turning out to have some nightmarish bursts in big-scale production.
There is another statement in the article which interested me because we are producing butyl in the plant at Sarnia. It says:
But the biggest "if" of all in the rubber programme is butyl, the synthetic from which inner tubes were to come. Ex-Trust-Buster Thurman Arnold once hailed butyl as the king of all rubber synthetics, and roundly denounced Standard Oil (N.J.) for not putting it on the market. Standard's prompt protests that butyl was not perfected -went unheard. But butyl, which was once programmed to supply 75,000 tons a year, proved Standard right, Arnold wrong. It is strangled in the intricacies of manufacture.
It seems to me that these are very interesting points. The article, of course, may not be accurate; I do not know about that; but it seems to be well posted, and so far as I know its accuracy has not been challenged, or, if it has, this has not been brought to my attention. I should like to know from the minister whether or not the plant at Sarnia has been proven to be a complete success, and that while in the United States they are having difficulty with synthetic rubber production, nevertheless in this country we are completely successful. I should also like to know that in connection with butyl rubber, which is the only kind that can be used for inner tubes, we have nothing to worry about. I sincerely hope
War Appropriation-Supplies

that the belief of the minister that the difficulties have been completely overcome will be justified1 by the facts, because this is a most important matter for the Canadian people and for Canadian economy, and it seems to me from the reports we get from the United States that there-is sufficient doubt about the process to warrant the administration continuing actively to canvass the question of a more intensive production of industrial alcohol from agricultural products to supplement, if necessary, the present programme, and at the same time give the agricultural areas of the west a use for their surplus products which cannot find their way into foodstuffs.

I should like to ask the minister a question which was raised this afternoon but to which I do not think an answer was given. I refer to the Sutton-Horsley plant, where the minister put in a controller by the name of Pinchin. The International Association of Machinists has complained that this controller has cut the number of workers from 1,200 to 400, and the rumour is that the entire plant is going to close down. I understand that they are making gauges for aircraft and for other purposes. Naturally a considerable amount of concern is felt by the workers in that plant.
The minister has not said anything about the effectiveness or otherwise of the utilization of machine shops, particularly in the mines, in making war material. There was quite a programme at one time to have the machine shops of the various mining companies making certain types of equipment as subcontractors for war industry. Has this programme been carried out; if so, to what extent, and has it been successful?
The parliamentary assistant to the mniister spoke this afternoon of the audit of fixed price contracts and said that when it was found upon investigation of a fixed price contract that a large or unnecessary profit was being made, after an audit of the company's operations a new price was agreed upon and made retroactive. I think the committee would like to have a little more detail of the methods of that process. Let us say that a base price of 100 units is fixed, and that at the end of the first three months operations the company produces material for eighty units of cost, making a profit of twenty units. Assuming that we consider that five per cent is a sufficient profit; there is a fifteen per cent excess profit, shall we say, over the fixed price. What is the machinery set up? Does the government go into that factory and say:	We want the fifteen
units of profit that you have made over the last three months? Or does it say: You can keep that excess profit and we will now allow

you eighty-five units of cost? I think the committee would be interested to have that information with regard to the revampnig of the fixed price contracts.
I believe the committee would also be interested in having information with regard to the cost of production of aircraft. We know it is impossible in the early stages to give any idea of the cost of production of aircraft. It is very difficult even to set a target price for aircraft when you are starting on the manufacture of a complicated air frame such as the Lancaster or the Mosquito. What I should like to know, however, and what I think the committee would like to know, is what is done as to a reduction in price for the manufacture of the Lancaster and the Mosquito as the programme has proceeded. I think the minister said that forty-nine Lancasters have been built-
I said thirty-nine.

Probably the base cost can now be obtained and some estimate of future cost arrived at. I think that is information which it is legitimate for the committee and the country to have.
With regard to the re-negotiation of cost-plus contracts. The cost-plus contract is, I suppose, a necessary evil in war time. It must happen when you are dealing with new operation, new factories on which no base rate can possibly be known. But when a base rate is known in the operation and a reasonable estimate can be made of the cost of the operation, even one as complicated as the building of aircraft or' the operation at Research Enterprise Limited, what is the machinery here again for re-negotiation of these cost-plus contracts?
I have one suggestion to make to the minister. During the war we have developed a number of strategic minerals. I shall not go through the list; they are well known to the committee. Ore bodies were- delimited and discovered, and actual production took place in many instances. We now find that because of the easing of the supply, or because of the bringing in of supplies from elsewhere, these operations are no longer economically feasible for the country to carry out. I speak in particular of the Emerald mine, the tungsten deposit in British Columbia. Apparently the mine is now closed down. We have developed an operation -which, because tungsten can be produced cheaper, in greater volume, or for other reasons in the United States, is now closed down. With all metals, their use depends upon the amount of research that goes into the work on them. It is well known that after the last war the International Nickel company found itself with a terrific production of nickel and no market. They

War Appropriation-Supplies
went and carried out by themselves one of the most intensive research programmes ever known on this continent. In consequence, not only did the demand for nickel come back to where it was in the last war, but it tremendously increased. I believe there were developed something like 250 separate alloys containing nickel, and to-day there is hardly an industry, hardly a machine, which does not contain this vitally important metal. Now, it seems to me that we, having developed these strategic metals, unless we can provide through research a use and a market for them, shall find ourselves with a development which is closed down and in which our investment as a country is lost. I suggest to the minister that one of the first priorities is to see to it that adequate research is carried out now so that new uses for these strategic minerals and metals can be found. That is an essential and important move at this stage of the war.
There has been a considerable discussion this afternoon on cartels. I was interested to note that the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation mentioned Canadian Industries-the I. G. Farbenindustrie-Imperial Chemical and du Pont. I brought this matter up in the house early in February. I think that, when we are dealing with something as abstract as cartels something which can be so misrepresented, and as to which so much misinformation can be injected, some statement might be forthcoming in this chamber concerning international cartels. I wish to quote two paragraphs from a paper delivered at the annual meeting of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy this month by Professor George B. Langford, professor of mining geology, University of Toronto. Dealing with cartels in the mineral industry, he has this to say:
Cartels and monopolies have existed, and now exist, in the mineral industries. Some have been outstandingly successful and others equally unsuccessful. When the time comes to put into effect the mineral industry policy advanced here, the history of the international metal cartels will be a useful guide in working out details, rnd also in pointing out pitfalls to be avoided. For the purpose of this discussion, only the oriefest mention will be made of some of the features of such organizations that are of interest in formulating a post-war mineral control policy.
Outstanding is the International Nickel Company of Canada, a virtual monopoly controlling SO to 9Q per cent of the world's supply of the' metal. Since 1926. this company has found it advantageous to maintain a fixed price for the metal, irrespective of violent fluctuations in general economic conditions. It has also adjusted its production to meet market demands and thus has prevented over-production.
The tin cartel, an association of individual companies brought together by international agreements, was sponsored by the governments
of the several producing nations. It has been referred to as the most successful metal cartel. It was formed in 1933 as the only logical cure for a badly disorganized and over-produced industry. Previous to its formation there had been several other curative methods tried without success. The object of the tin cartel was stated in the first clause of the agreement for the international tin control scheme:	"The
scheme is intended to secure a fair and reasonable relation between production and consumption with a view to prevent rapid and severe oscillations of prices and to ensure the absorption of surplus stock."
The operations of this cartel proved the feasibility of international political- control in mineral industries.
The aluminum industry in North America has operated as a monopoly because of cartel agreements with European producers. This monopoly has not always operated in the best interests of the consumers, and demonstrates the inadvisability of leaving the operations of such organizations without suitable controls.
Professor Langford goes on to mention copper cartels and other cartels which have failed. I merely mention this to show that cartels, as a method of regulating mineral production and as a method of preventing violent swings of price and instability of employment, and for other reasons, are not always a bad and vicious thing, and I mention here the tin cartel as an example.
1 had not intended to speak at such length, but in view of what has been said this afternoon I brought this up.

It is not my intention to make a speech, but I would ask the minister a question or two. First, I should like to ask him whether any cooperative organizations, especially Cooperative Implements Limited, made any representations or request to his department or to the government with a view to obtaining from the government those surpluses he referred to the other day when he was speaking, or possibly even the disposing of those surpluses after the close of hostilities. If they have made representations, I would ask him whether his department or the government are prepared to give any consideration to these requests at the present time.
Many of us farmers feel keenly about this, because for quite a number of years now we have found ourselves severely handicapped in eariying on our farming operations, first through inability to purchase the new machinery we required owing to the prices we were receiving for our products; and later on, now that we do have a little money to buy the necessary machines, we find ourselves unable to get them because the machines are not there or there are not enough to go around. To make matters worse, after we had become quite adapted to the repairing of our machines out of our scrap-heaps, along came an order
War Appropriation-Supplies

from one of the boards under the minister compelling us to dispose of our scrap metal which we had on our farms, leaving us only a very limited amount of scrap with which to continue repairing our machines.
Some of us felt rather hot under the collar when we were forced to deliver our scrap for $7 a ton, much of which we had to pay S700 a ton for when we bought it.
Who used the force that made the hon. gentleman deliver the scrap?

There were different advertisements in the newspapers, in my part of the country at any rate, that gave us up to a certain time to have that scrap delivered at certain places, failing which there would be penalties if we were found with more scrap than a certain number of pounds on our farms. I am sorry I have not the advertisements here, but I am sure the minister must know something about it.
Did you deliver the scrap iron?

I certainly did. It cost me more in time gathering the stuff and hauling it than I got out of it on top of all the other misery, and then we had not what we needed to keep on repairing our machinery. Incidentally, some of these scrap heaps were lying around the railway sidings for quite a time. But I am not arguing about that. I realize that, under the circumstances, the boards may have justification in calling in that scrap, and in spite of the fact that we delivered scrap for $7 a ton, which cost in some instances $700 a ton when we bought the implements, nevertheless we were prepared to do that. We consider, however, that some of this surplus equipment, it may be in the line of trucks, or jeeps or other equipment; it may be even in some of the plants in which the government is interested, might be made available to the farmers so that they might get the necessary material at reasonable cost.
If the minister would rather discuss this question when he is before the house with the bill to which he referred the other day, dealing with the Assets Disposal Corporation, I am prepared to let the matter stand until then. In the meantime, I would impress upon him that the farmers in the west expect that as soon as possible their cooperative organizations shall be given an opportunity to take part in handling some of that equipment, at least so far as it is adaptable to agricultural purposes.

I am suspicious of people who say they are not going to make a speech, like the hon. gentleman, who made a good job of it. In regard

to scrap metal on the farms, I know that in our section of the country there were notices in the newspapers, but our farmers never figured on anything for the scrap. They gave it to the Red Cross Society.
In the minister's speech it appears that of small craft, 3,600 were delivered out of a total of 4,300 orders placed, and the rate of deliveries in 1944 will be about the same as 1943. I should like to know from the minister where those small craft were delivered. In one newspaper item the statement is made "Landing craft a big item now in shipbuilding". I asked the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) on March 17 a question in regard to small craft. I said:
What about landing craft and seeps?
The minister replied:
No, not for our navy.
Where did those go to? Did Canada get any of those delivered, or were they all for the United States and Great Britain?
Is the hon. member speaking of landing craft?
Landing craft, jeeps, seeps, ducks and other small boats of that kind.

Quite a number were delivered to the Canadian navy. All landing craft were delivered in the United Kingdom, but I believe all our small boats programme was divided between the Canadian navy and the British navy.
Why would the Minister for Naval Services make that statement? I asked, "What about landing craft and seeps?" and he distinctly said, "No, not for our navy".
Did the hon. member mean the assault craft?
The seeps are the ones that can go on land and water.
We are not building any. Perhaps my hon. friend is referring to the landing craft.
The ones with open bow?
L.S.T. type.
A large type or a small type?
We are building the large type at the moment. We are building the type called the L.S.T., which is a very large type.

What tonnage would that be?

War Appropriation-Supplies
Quite large, perhaps eight or ten thousand tons.
Could I obtain under this item answers to my questions in connection with synthetic rubber plants?
I think I made a statement this afternoon that covered the entire field of the questions asked by my hon. friend.

No. I should like to ask the minister the reason why last year he stated he anticipated that the plant would come into full production by November, and now he says it will not come into full production until July after the butyl production is brought up a considerable amount. Was there any particular reason why there was that delay?
The plant was in production last November.
Yes, I know.

In production before that. Full production means, of course, every unit operating at capacity, and it is not up to that now. As Time magazine stated-and it was quite correct with regard to one feature- butyl production turned out to be a very difficult process. As I stated this afternoon, we planned these plants before buna-S or butyl rubber had ever been produced on this continent outside of a laboratory. It was believed in the early stages that it would be easier to make butyl than buna-S. It turned out in practice that there were difficulties in large scale operation in connection with butyl, but those have been overcome and butyl production is stepping up very satisfactorily.

Last year the minister stated that he anticipated the production of butyl would be eight thousand tons. The other day he said four thousand tons. Is that because of the difficulty that we have run into in connection with the production?
No, I do not think so. I am not sure whether the figure is four thousand or eight thousand. Perhaps the eight thousand figure was wrong. Whatever we planned originally will be produced.
According to the minister's statement of last year eight thousand tons were planned originally. I was wondering why four thousand tons were mentioned in the statement the other day.

I do not think the unit was dropped. It may have been dropped, but I do not think so. I shall get the answer and give it to my hon. friend. I think I was correct in the first statement that we shall
eventually have eight thousand tons of butyl, but sometimes changes are made. I do not recall a change in that particular capacity. Sometimes we slip from one product to another while we are building the plant, but I shall look into the facts of the matter as to butyl.	*
Has the minister any information about the plant at Sutton-Horsley?

Yes, Sutton-Horsley was a small operation stepped up into a very large operation. We had a need for a large number of instruments for trainer aircraft and a contract was given to Sutton-Horsley. Considerable advances of working capital were made and it was found that the finances of the company were being badly handled. The inventory on hand did not represent the advances made. We therefore put in a controller in the person of Mr. Pinchin to straighten out the operation, and particularly the finances of the company. He succeeded in doing that. All the operating capital put in by the government was recovered and the receivership was ended. The fact that the work has dropped off recently is on account of the falling off in the production of trainer planes. They have dropped sharply as a result of the curtailment of the air training programme, and the future of the existing contracts depends entirely on the future production of trainer aircraft in this country.
Would the minister care to discuss the question to which I referred?

Yes. We had representations from this cooperative. The representations were turned over to the crown assets allocation committee. The difficulty at the moment is that no department of government has declared agricultural implements or anything resembling them a surplus; therefore we have nothing to send to the cooperative at the moment. Their request is on file, and as soon as we have the type of implement in which they are interested we shall be glad to have their help and the help of other cooperatives in distributing the production in the area in which they operate.

On page 5 of the report made available to members to-day appears an item for Frost and Wood of $281,146. I understand that this company at Smiths Falls has recently received an order for a thousand reapers and some work has been done on retooling. I wonder if an order of that kind would come through Munitions and Supply and, if so, what country at this stage of the world's history is going back to the reaper? Are we to make it possible for tight materials
War Appropriation-Supplies

to be made available for the making of reapers? Has the minister any information about that?

I may say that Frost and Wood had a contract through my department for making gun carriages, I think it was. I believe that contract has been completed. I am sure that if they have a contract for reapers it is a contract they received through the ordinary channels of trade. My department does not buy reapers.

Is there not a department concerned about the releasing of tight materials for the manufacture of an article like the reaper? Surely it should be a matter of government concern as to whether or not Canadian workmen and Canadian materials are to be used for the manufacture of reapers?
There is no tight material situation associated with that type of production.

Farmers across the
country are being told that there is a serious shortage of all the materials used in the manufacture of farm implements. If we can release materials for the manufacture of reapers I should imagine that those materials should be made available for other much more necessary instruments of production. I have not seen a reaper in operation during my lifetime. It seems a pity that workmen and materials should be used, if my information is right, in the manufacture of reapers.
I really cannot say. That contract was not placed by the Department of Munitions and Supply. I do not know the story.
Has the minister any information about the cost of aircraft?
Are we to understand that there is no longer a shortage of material used in farm implements?
That is correct.
Are we to have all the instruments we need?
I did not say that. If you cannot get them it is not a matter of materials being in short supply.

I notice farm implements are rationed and we have quite a few complaints coming in of people not being able to buy the implements. If the materials are there, it would be a good idea to put the workmen to work.

If my hon. friend can find any spare manufacturing capacity I am sure we

shall be glad to use it for that purpose. The industry is working at full capacity at the moment.
The price of aeroplanes is not a subject to discuss in five minutes. If my hon. friend is interested in the price of aircraft I shall take fifteen minutes to-morrow and give a lecture on the subject.

I think it would be interesting in view of the policy the minister has brought down in regard to post-war civil aviation. It might be a complementary subject which would be of interest to the hon. members.

I shall be very glad to do that, but it is not a subject on which you can say, what does this plane cost? To take a figure and compare it with the cost of another plane somewhere else, and then to decide that one plant is doing much better than another. I will show how the manufacturing costs of aeroplanes vary with the size of the contract and the range of the run, the number of units produced. After that I shall be glad to discuss costs, but I think it is important to have a background.
That is what I hoped the minister would do, and in the same way I should like to get some information from the parliamentary assistant with reference to the methods of reallocating contracts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think I can give my hon. friend that now. He spoke first of all of the cost-plus contract, which he said was a necessary evil. That is true; but it is a fact also that we have tried in the department to get away from cost-plus percentage contracts, and we have done very well over a period of time. I went on to discuss this afternoon the main purchasing branches of the department, and I think I showed how, in each of those, the percentage had gone down tremendously. Last year I was able to say that four-sevenths, in point of number, of contracts granted in the department were on a fixed price basis. This year there are substantially more than that. I do not know what they are, in point of numbers, but there are certainly five-sevenths, if not six-sevenths.
Then, with reference to re-negotiation, renegotiation is brought about by our cost accountants, who are stationed in plants and who, when they have evidence of undue profits, re-negotiate immediately. The re-negotiation in the department is a retroactive re-negotiation. That is, it is one which dates back to the original date of the contract. In other words, if a re-negotiation begins now-to-day-and we find there is undue profit, the price will

War Appropriation-Supplies
revert to the date of the original contract. This afternoon I compared our system with that in Australia, where re-negotiation is not retrospective, and dates from the time of renegotiation. I believe those are the two questions which were asked.

That is the question in which I am interested. If, because of increased efficiency in a plant, the manufacturing cost comes down, and undue profit is being made, it might be that undue profit was not being made at the beginning of the contract because the operation was not handled as efficiently as it was six months later. Then the department re-negotiates at the beginning of the contract, and reduces the price of the article from that time. It seems to me that the department is going to cause considerable loss, if it does that, because the first period of production might have been nearer the fixed price allotted by the department. Only after six months, or a period of time has elapsed, and because of increased efficiency is an undue profit being made. It seems to me that if they are made retroactive, the department will be paying less than the article actually cost during the first period of the contract. It appears to me that there is that danger.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
That is exactly what we have done, that is, we re-negotiate them as of the date of the original contract.
While I am on my feet perhaps I can answer before 'eleven o'clock some of the questions asked this afternoon and this evening. The hon. member for Lake Centre asked for some particulars with respect to re-negotiation. He wanted to know the numbers. There are eighty-three re-negotiations which have taken place. The value of those re-negotiations amounts to $119,107,000. Then, with reference to the number of cancellations of contracts, m3' hon. friend will appreciate that cancellations have to do not only with prime contractors but also with subcontractors, and therefore it is impossible to obtain the information. I cannot give him the number of those.
While I was speaking he asked me to give the percentage of profit allowed to aircraft operating companies. In the department we aim at five per cent. Sometimes it is under that, and sometimes over. But the profit is in the order of five per cent, with something better in certain cases where unusual skill has been shown, and something less in other cases. There are also some occasions where the fee is fixed. For instance, there is the cost plus a fixed fee.

How much does
"something more" amount to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It depends upon the
circumstances, and I am not in a position to give any further details. As I said before, the target is five per cent. We aim at cost plus five per cent. There are cases where it is under that amount, and other cases where it is over.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked some questions yesterday with respect to the subsidy on wood fuel. * The total production subsidy is $757,664.15. This represents a payment. of one dollar a cord on all commercial wood fuel cut on or before March 1, 1944, and delivered to a dealer or held to his account after March 5, 1943. In addition to the production subsidy, transportation subsidies amounting to $257,639.71 have been paid. These pa>unents cover such portion of the transportation costs incurred by wood-fuel dealers in the transportation of wood fuel. Both of these subsidies are paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation on receipt of a certification by the wood-fuel controller.
The hon. member for- York-Sunbury also asked what quota of heavy-duty trucks are being imported into Canada.
How is the subsidy on transportation arrived at?

If wood is required in an area, and must be brought in from outside the normal sources, the transportation bonus is paid, representing the difference between the normal cost of transportation and the actual cost paid from the greater distance. We had a situation that represented, among other things, a very bad distribution of wood. The normal sources could not be developed sufficiently to produce the required supplies and, as I say, we went outside the area. For instance, at the head of the lakes we cut 75,000 cords of wood as a reserve supply for points both east and west of the head of the lakes. That is not a normal operation; it was an emergency. And moving wood from that emergency store, either to Winnipeg or to the east, involved an abnormal cost that was covered by the transportation bonus.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Perhaps I might continue. I had referred to the question by the hon. member for York-Sunbury as to the quota of heavy-duty trucks being imported into Canada. The answer is that heavy-duty trucks of 16,000 pounds or over, gross vehicle weight rating, are not produced in Canada. The quota of imports from the United States is fixed by the motor vehicles controller in consultation with the director of the automotive division of the war production board in the United States. The quota in 1943 was seventy-four; the quota in 1944 is 207.

Then the hon. member for Peterborough West asked a question with respect to glycerine. The answer is that glycerine is now on the free list, by virtue of order CC-2-B-3 of December 31, 1943. At that time all restrictions on glycerine were lifted.
The minister will remember that he undertook to bring down a statement with regard to the processing of coal at the mine. Will he be good enough to make a statement to-morrow?

My hon. friend spoke about processing coal at the mine head. We are doing no processing of that type in Canada at this time. But the Department of Mines and Resources are continuing studies on the hydrogenation of coal at this time. In fact a special laboratory has been built for that purpose. The subject matter will be considered very carefully. It is appreciated that it would be a favourable way to deal with some of the western mines, particularly if it turns out to be an economical process. We are hoping that some progress may be made.
It has not got beyond the experimental stage?

No.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
